In [[linear algebra]], a '''constrained generalized inverse''' is obtained by solving a [[system of linear equations]] with an additional constraint that the solution is in a given subspace. One also says that the problem is described by a system of [[Linear least squares (mathematics)#Constrained linear least squares|constrained linear equations]].

In many practical problems, the solution <math>x</math> of a linear system of equations
:<math>
Ax=b\qquad (\text{with given }A\in\R^{m\times n}\text{ and } b\in\R^m)
</math>
is acceptable only when it is in a certain [[linear subspace]] <math>L</math> of <math>\R^n</math>.

In the following, the [[orthogonal projection]] on <math>L</math> will be denoted by  <math>P_L</math>.
Constrained system of linear equations
:<math>Ax=b\qquad x\in L</math>
has a solution if and only if the unconstrained system of equations 
:<math>(A P_L) x = b\qquad x\in\R^n</math>
is solvable. If the subspace <math>L</math> is a proper subspace of <math>\R^n</math>, then the matrix of the unconstrained problem <math>(A P_L)</math> may be singular even if the system matrix <math>A</math> of the constrained problem is invertible (in that case, <math>m=n</math>). This means that one needs to use a generalized inverse for the solution of the constrained problem. So, a generalized inverse of <math>(A P_L)</math> is also called a <math>L</math>-''constrained pseudoinverse'' of <math>A</math>.

An example of a pseudoinverse that can be used for the solution of a constrained problem is the '''Bott–Duffin inverse''' of <math>A</math> constrained to <math>L</math>, which is defined by the equation
:<math>A_L^{(-1)}:=P_L(A P_L + P_{L^\perp})^{-1},</math>
if the inverse on the right-hand-side exists.
